summary: Announces a mail server at UCSB listening on socket 3 that implements the small part of FTP needed to deliver mail: the MAIL and BYE commands. It lists the UCSB users who could receive network mail and their user names.

plainLanguage.summary: A university computer opened a mailbox for the network. You could send letters to a short list of people there, and this note names them.

questions: how did early ftp mail delivery work
subtitle: Announcing network mail capability at a new server.

tldr.problem: Before this announcement, it was difficult to send mail to users at UCSB over the ARPANET.
tldr.mechanism: UCSB set up a server on socket 3 that implements just enough of the FTP protocol to support mail delivery: the MAIL and BYE commands.
tldr.outcome: Mail could now be sent to six specific UCSB users and a general complaints address (GRIPE), using FTP's simple mail delivery mechanism.

today: RFC 574 is a historical announcement of an early mail service. It is not a specification or standard.

sections.title: The UCSB Mail Server
sections.content: UCSB has set up a mail server program listening on socket 3 that implements the minimal subset of the File Transfer Protocol needed for mail delivery. Instead of implementing the full FTP specification, the server supports only two commands: MAIL (to send a message to a recipient) and BYE (to end the connection). This simplified approach makes mail delivery straightforward and reliable.
sections.plainLanguage: UCSB created a special computer program that accepts mail sent over the network. It only understands two commands: deliver this mail, and goodbye.

sections.title: How to Send Mail to UCSB
sections.content: Mail may be sent to an individual at UCSB by using the MAIL command and specifying their local user name. Six individuals are defined as valid recipients: Ed Faeh (FAEH), Jim Guyton (GUYTON), Mark Krilanovich (KRILANOV), Curtis Mosso (MOSSO), John Pickens (PICKENS), and Ron Stoughton (STOUGHTN). In addition, any general comments or complaints about UCSB services may be sent to the special user name GRIPE.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send mail to any of six specific people at UCSB, or to a general feedback address called GRIPE.

sections.title: Significance
sections.content: This service represents an early example of cross-network mail delivery using a minimal subset of FTP. By implementing only the essential MAIL and BYE commands, UCSB created a simple, robust mail gateway. This approach contrasts with full FTP server implementations while still providing useful mail functionality to ARPANET users wanting to contact specific individuals at the institution.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a simple way to let people on the network send mail to UCSB without having to set up a complicated system.
